blocks.text: **A retry is the same call made again after it fails, in the hope that what went wrong has passed.**

A call across a network can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the request: a dropped connection, a server busy for a moment. Faults like these are transient: they pass^1. Trying again turns many of them into successes, at the cost of a little time.

A retry is only safe when doing the work twice does no more harm than doing it once. An operation that can be repeated as often as needed without unintended effects is called idempotent^2, and a call that isn’t needs something that makes it so before it is retried.

claims.text: Faults are classed by how long they last, permanent or transient.

quotes.text: Faults are commonly categorized by their locality (internal or external to the system), cause (natural or human-made), duration (permanent or transient), and effect on system behavior.

claims.words: Faults like these are transient: they pass

claims.text: An idempotent operation can be repeated or retried as often as needed without unintended effects.

quotes.text: This is a very useful property in many situations, as it means that an operation can be repeated or retried as often as necessary without causing unintended effects.

claims.words: An operation that can be repeated as often as needed without unintended effects is called idempotent

blocks.text: A client sends a payment and the connection drops before any answer comes. It waits a moment and sends the same request again. If the first one never arrived, the payment goes through now; if it did, the server must see that this is the same payment, not a second one.

A transient fault is a fault that lasts only a moment and clears by itself: a dropped connection, a service briefly unavailable, a timeout while a server is busy. Trying the same operation again a little later usually works. The hard part is telling these apart from failures that will happen every time, however often you retry.

An online shop calls a payment service for each order. Every so often a call times out during a brief network blip, and the next call a moment later goes through. Failing the customer's order for that would lose a sale for nothing. But if the card was declined or the request was malformed, calling again will fail the same way, and only adds load. The shop needs to know which kind of failure it has.

Handling them has three parts: recognise the fault as transient, wait, and try again, within a limit. Microsoft's guidance lists transient faults as the momentary loss of network connectivity, the temporary unavailability of a service, and timeouts when a service is busy; they typically resolve without intervention, so the action is likely to succeed if retried after a suitable delay^1. They are most common in a distributed system, where every call crosses a network to a shared service.

Recognising them comes first: an application must detect faults and decide whether each is transient, long-lasting or terminal^1. Error responses usually say: a busy or temporarily unavailable service often returns a specific error code, while bad input or a refused permission does not change on a second try. Services can help by returning errors that tell clients whether to retry and how long to wait^1. Then comes the [[retry pattern]], with waits that grow by [[exponential backoff]]: the application waits a short time before the first retry, then increases the wait exponentially before each one after^1. Jitter, a small random delay added to each wait, stops many clients from retrying in step^1.

data.caption: Five layers of services, each trying three times, turn one failing request into 243 attempts on the database.

blocks.text: A call fails with a timeout. The client waits 100 milliseconds and tries again, then 200, then 400, then 800, giving up after four retries and about 1.5 seconds of waiting. With jitter, each wait is a random time up to that limit, so a thousand clients that failed together don't all return at the same instant. If the blip lasted 250 milliseconds, the first retry at 100 milliseconds fails and the second, at about 300, succeeds. If all four fail, the fault probably isn't transient, and the client reports an error instead of waiting longer.

An intermittent fault also comes and goes, so it can look transient. The difference is cause. A transient fault comes from passing conditions, such as a brief network drop; an intermittent fault keeps coming back from a real defect, such as a loose cable or a race condition. Retrying hides an intermittent fault without fixing it. The test is the pattern: if the same failure keeps returning, look for the defect instead of adding retries.

In a system made of many networked parts, something is always briefly failing, so treating every hiccup as fatal makes the whole system fragile. Retrying absorbs these hiccups cheaply. But retries add load just when a service is struggling, which is why they come with waits, randomness and limits. Microsoft recommends a retry budget, which limits the total retry load so many requests each retrying a few times don't together overwhelm a struggling service^1.

Retrying is only safe for operations that can be repeated, a property called [[idempotence]]. If an operation that increments a value runs twice, it gives a wrong result, so operations that aren't idempotent can leave data inconsistent when retried^1. Retries also add delay for the user, and a fault that turns out to be long-lasting turns every request into a slow failure.

The belief: if retrying helps, retry at every layer. Retries multiply. AWS describes a five-deep stack of service calls ending in a database, with three retries at each layer: if each layer retries on its own, the load on the database rises 243 times, making it unlikely ever to recover^2. What is true: for low-cost control-plane and data-plane operations, AWS's best practice is to retry at a single point in the stack^2, and let the other layers fail fast.

Treat a failure as a permanent fault and fail fast when trying again can't help, as with invalid input or a missing permission. When a service keeps failing, a [[circuit breaker pattern]] stops calling it for a while, so callers get a quick error instead of waiting through retries, and the service gets room to recover. Most systems combine all three: retries for transient faults, fast failure for permanent ones, and a circuit breaker for faults that last.

sources.title: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

blocks.text: Exponential backoff is a rule for how long to wait before retrying something that failed. After each failure the wait is multiplied, usually doubled: 1 second, then 2, then 4. Early retries come quickly, while a service that stays down gets fewer and fewer requests from each client.

A storage service is overloaded and starts returning errors: it has [[network congestion]], more arriving than it can handle. A thousand clients each retry at once, then again, so it gets more traffic than before the trouble began. When failures come from overload, retries that add load can make matters much worse, and can delay recovery by keeping load high after the cause has gone^1. Retrying immediately or with very short delays can lead to cascading failures^2.

Backoff is a kind of [[retry pattern]] with three parts: a first wait, a multiplier and a cap. Instead of retrying at once, the client waits between tries, and the wait grows exponentially after every attempt^1. That [[exponential growth]] gets long fast, so implementations usually cap the wait at a maximum, which AWS calls capped exponential backoff^1. Google's guidance describes the same scheme: exponentially increasing waits between requests, up to a maximum backoff time^2.

A fourth part, [[jitter]], fixes a flaw. If every client that failed at the same moment backs off by the same amount, they all retry together and cause the overload again^1, a form of the [[thundering herd problem]]. Jitter adds randomness to each wait to spread the retries out in time^1, and Google advises generally using exponential backoff with jitter for requests that meet its response and idempotency criteria^2. A [[timeout]] decides when an attempt counts as failed; backoff decides when to try again.

Take a first wait of 1 second, a multiplier of 2 and a cap of 32 seconds. The waits run 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, then 32 seconds again. After six failures a client has waited 63 seconds in all, and from then on sends one request every 32 seconds instead of one a second. If each wait is instead a random time between zero and that figure, the sixth wait might be 11 seconds for one client and 27 for another, so they no longer arrive together.

Retrying after a fixed delay, constant backoff, looks similar in code but never eases off: a client keeps sending one request every interval however long the outage lasts. Backoff is only exponential if the wait is multiplied after each failure.

The principle is that retries are selfish: a client that retries spends more of the server's time to raise its own chance of success^1. That's fine when failures are rare, but in a distributed system there's almost no way for all the clients to agree on the right number of retries^1. Doubling waits let each client halve its own load after every failure with no coordination at all, so total load falls fastest exactly when the service is most stressed.

A capped backoff leaves every client retrying steadily at the cap, so AWS also limits the number of retries and handles the failure earlier^1. Retries in layers multiply: five layers each retrying three times can raise the load on a database 243-fold^1. Backoff only helps with errors that might pass: errors such as invalid requests are persistent, and retrying them without fixing the cause won't succeed^2. And every retry repeats the request, so it must be safe to repeat, which is what [[idempotence]] guarantees.

A [[circuit breaker]] stops calls to a downstream service entirely once errors pass a threshold; choose it when a service is down for long. AWS notes it can make systems harder to test and add significant time to recovery^1. When the server knows when it will be ready, a Retry-After header tells the client how long to wait before trying again, and with a 503 response says how long the service expects to be unavailable^3. A fixed delay suits only brief, rare failures that retries can't make worse.

blocks.text: Jitter is randomness added to the wait before a retry, so that clients which failed together do not all retry together. Instead of every client waiting exactly 4 seconds, each waits a random time up to 4 seconds. It refines a [[retry strategy]] by spreading the retries around in time.^1

A database stalls for a second and 1,000 clients fail at once. With [[exponential backoff]], each waits 1 second, then 2, then 4, but all 1,000 wait the same amounts. If all the failed calls back off to the same time, they cause contention or overload again when they retry.^1 This is the [[thundering herd problem]]: backoff makes calls less frequent, but there are still clusters of calls.^2

Jitter has three parts: a backoff schedule, a cap and a random draw. Capped exponential backoff multiplies the wait by a constant after each attempt, up to some maximum.^2 Jitter then replaces that computed wait with a random one. In the variant Marc Brooker calls Full Jitter, each client sleeps a random time between zero and the computed wait.
The figure shows one round of it: 100 clients that failed together, each about to wait up to 8 seconds before trying again.

data.describe: Retries arriving in each half second from 100 clients that failed at the same moment, each waiting up to 8 seconds. Without jitter, all 100 arrive together at 8 seconds. With full jitter, in one run, they arrive spread across the 8 seconds, never more than 10 in any half second.

blocks.text: Two other variants keep more of the schedule. Equal Jitter always keeps some of the backoff and adds a smaller random amount, and Decorrelated Jitter raises the maximum based on the last random value.^2 In Brooker's simulation, Equal Jitter did slightly more work than Full Jitter and took much longer.^2

Take 4 clients that failed at the same moment, on their third retry with a base wait of 1 second. Plain backoff gives each a wait of 4 seconds, so all 4 retry at once. Full Jitter gives each a random wait between 0 and 4 seconds, say 0.7, 1.9, 2.6 and 3.8, and the server sees them one at a time. In Brooker's simulation with 100 contending clients, adding jitter cut the number of calls by more than half and shortened the time to finish.^2

The belief: exponential backoff on its own prevents retry storms. Why it's wrong: in Brooker's simulation, backoff helped only a small amount and did not solve the problem.^2 What's true: the answer is not to remove backoff but to add jitter to it.^2

The problem is correlation: clients that failed from one cause share one schedule. [[Randomness]] breaks that link. With jitter the gaps disappear, and after the first spike the calls arrive at an approximately constant rate, which a server copes with far better.^2 Brooker admits it can seem counter-intuitive to improve performance by adding randomness, but concludes that jittered backoff should be a standard approach for remote clients.^2
Network jitter, the variation in how long packets take to arrive, shares the name but is something a system suffers, not something it adds. Retry jitter is chosen on purpose.

Jitter changes when retries happen, not how many. Retries themselves multiply load: with a database at the end of five layers of calls, each retrying three times, the load on the database can rise 243 times.^1 And every retried request must be safe to repeat, the property called [[idempotence]]. For scheduled work, AWS avoids purely random jitter, using a value that stays the same on each host, so that problems recur in a pattern people can spot.^1

A token bucket on the client lets calls retry while tokens remain, then only at a fixed rate,^1 which bounds how many retries go out at all. [[Rate limiting]] on the server caps load however clients time their retries. A [[circuit breaker]] stops calling a failing service for a while, though it brings modal behaviour that can be hard to test.^1

blocks.text: An idempotency key is a unique value a client sends with a request, such as a payment, so that the server can recognise the same request if it arrives again. The server does the work the first time, saves its answer under the key, and sends that saved answer back for any repeat. So a client that is unsure whether a request got through can safely send it again.

Your app sends a request to create a £20 payment, and the connection drops before any reply. A client in that position cannot tell whether the payment was created, or whether the server even finished the request.^1 Sending it again risks a duplicate side effect, £40 charged in all; not sending it risks losing the sale. HTTP's own rules leave this to the API for creating things: GET, PUT and DELETE are [[idempotent]], but POST and PATCH are not.^1

Three parts make it work. First, the client generates the key, a unique identifier for this one intended action; the IETF draft on the subject recommends a UUID or a similar random identifier.^1 Stripe also warns against using sensitive data, such as email addresses, as keys.^2 Second, the client sends the key with the request, in the `Idempotency-Key` header, and the server uses it to recognise later retries of the same request.^1 Every [[retry]] carries the same key.

Third, the server remembers keys it has seen. For a key it has not seen, it should process the request normally.^1 For a retry that arrives after the original finished, it should answer as if the request had been completed as the user intended.^1 In Stripe's version 1 API, that means saving the status code and body of the first request with a key and returning that saved response to retries, even a 500 error.^2 The figure shows a lost reply.

data.describe: The client asks the server to create a payment with key 8e03. The server charges, saves the result under that key, and replies, but the reply is lost. The client retries with the same key, and the server returns the saved result without charging again.

blocks.text: A checkout sends a request to create a payment of `2000` pence with `Idempotency-Key: 8e03978e-40d5-43e8-bc93-6894a57f9324`. The server charges the card, stores its reply, `201 Created` with payment `pay_1`, under that key, and sends it. The reply is lost. Two seconds later the client sends the identical request. The server finds the key, skips the charge and returns the stored `201` with `pay_1`. The customer pays £20 once, and the client learns the payment exists.

Had the retry arrived while the first charge was still running, the server should have answered `409 Conflict`.^1 The client would then wait, with [[exponential backoff]], and send the same request and key again.

A request ID is not an idempotency key. Many APIs tag each request with an ID for logs and support, and a retry gets a new one. An idempotency key belongs to the intended action, the one payment, and stays the same across every attempt to make it.

Over a network, a lost reply looks just like a lost request, so a client can never be sure something did not happen. The only way not to lose work is to retry, which gives at-least-once delivery. The key makes those repeats harmless by moving the memory of what was done to the server, which can see it. It names the intent rather than the contents, so the server can tell a retry from a genuine second payment of the same amount.

The server must store each key and its result, so keys expire after a time to live. In Stripe's version 1 API, keys can be removed once they are at least 24 hours old, and a key reused after that starts a new request.^2 The IETF draft leaves expiry to each service, which should publish its policy.^1 Keys also help only where the server honours them: without knowing the server, a client cannot assume it will.^1

The belief: a fresh key for every attempt is safest. It is the opposite: a new key makes a retry look like a new request, and the server does the work again. Make the key once, when the user decides to pay, and keep it for every retry of that payment. Nor may one key be reused for a different request: Stripe returns an error if the parameters differ from the original,^2 and the draft says a service should answer 422 then.^1

items: Naturally idempotent operations: design the call so a repeat is harmless, such as setting a value rather than adding to it. Stripe says not to send keys with its GET and DELETE requests, which are idempotent by definition.^2 Pick this whenever the action can be phrased as setting state.

A conditional request carries the version the client last saw, such as an ETag, and is applied only if the resource still matches. A repeat finds the version changed and is refused. Pick it for updates to an existing resource, where it also catches conflicting edits.

blocks.text: **An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.**

Applying it again changes nothing beyond the first time^1. Setting a light to on is idempotent; flipping its switch is not. That is what makes an operation safe to repeat or retry as often as needed^1, and why systems that retry care about it.

claims.text: An idempotent operation can be applied many times without changing the result beyond the first.

quotes.text: is the property of certain operations in mathematics and computer science whereby they can be applied multiple times without changing the result beyond the initial application

claims.words: Applying it again changes nothing beyond the first time

claims.text: It means an operation can be repeated or retried as often as needed without unintended effects.

quotes.text: This is a very useful property in many situations, as it means that an operation can be repeated or retried as often as necessary without causing unintended effects.

claims.words: safe to repeat or retry as often as needed

blocks.text: **A timeout is a limit on how long to wait for an answer, after which the caller gives up and does something else.**

Rather than wait for ever for something that may never happen, the wait ends when the time is up^1. A call to a service that has hung would otherwise hold its caller, and everything waiting on it, indefinitely.
Choosing the limit is hard: too short and healthy calls fail early, too long and failures are slow to show^1.

claims.text: A timeout aborts a wait instead of waiting indefinitely.

quotes.text: The basic idea is that in situations where a system must wait for something to happen, rather than waiting indefinitely, the waiting will be aborted after the timeout period has elapsed.

claims.words: Rather than wait for ever for something that may never happen, the wait ends when the time is up

claims.text: Short timeouts fail healthy requests; long ones make errors slow.

quotes.text: short timeout values can fail healthy requests prematurely, leading to complex workarounds, while long timeout values can result in slow error responses and poor user experiences

claims.words: too short and healthy calls fail early, too long and failures are slow to show

blocks.text: **An authorisation hold sets money aside for a payment first, and takes it only when the payment is settled.**

The card’s provider puts a hold on the amount, so the funds can’t be spent twice, until the merchant settles the transaction or the hold runs out^1. It is a payment in two steps, an authorisation and a settlement, with time between them^1.

claims.text: A hold reduces the available funds until the transaction is settled or the hold expires.

quotes.text: puts a hold of the amount approved by the cardholder, reducing the balance of available funds until the merchant clears the transaction (also called settlement), after the transaction is completed or aborted, or because the hold expires

claims.words: It is a payment in two steps, an authorisation and a settlement, with time between them

blocks.text: **In double-entry bookkeeping, every movement of money is written down twice: once where it leaves, once where it arrives, in equal and opposite amounts.**

Because each transaction is a debit and a matching credit, the books always balance^1, and an entry missing its pair shows up as an error^1. A ledger kept this way never stores a balance: an account’s balance is the sum of its entries.

claims.text: Every transaction is recorded with equal and opposite entries, so the books balance.

quotes.text: is a method of bookkeeping in which every financial transaction is recorded with equal and opposite entries (debits and credits) - thus "balancing the books"

blocks.text: **A database transaction groups several changes so they happen together or not at all, and keeps them apart from other work going on at the same time.**

Moving money is the usual example: taking an amount from one account and adding it to another is one transaction^1. If it stopped halfway, money would vanish. Transactions also keep programs working on the database at the same moment from seeing each other’s half-finished work^1.

blocks.text: **A change is atomic when it can’t be split: all of it happens, or none of it does.**
A transaction made of several operations is atomic if they all occur or none occur^1. That rules out partial updates, which cause more trouble than refusing the whole change would^1.

quotes.text: is the property of a database transaction consisting of an indivisible and irreducible series of database operations such that either all occur, or none occur

blocks.text: **An advisory lock is a lock that only works because everyone agrees to take it before touching what it guards.**

Most locks are advisory: each thread takes the lock before it reaches the data, by cooperation^1. Nothing stops code that skips the lock, unlike a mandatory lock, which refuses access outright^1. A database can keep advisory locks under names a program chooses, such as one per customer, so two charges for the same customer never run at once.

One thread never enters that critical section while another is in it^1. Without it, two changes made at once can leave shared data in a state neither intended. Dijkstra first set out and solved the problem in 1965^1.

It mixes a cryptographic hash function with the secret^1, and checks both that the data is intact and that it is authentic^1. Both sides share the same key, so no public key infrastructure is needed^1: a bank signing its webhooks with a secret it shares with you is the usual case.

An ordinary comparison stops at the first difference, so a wrong guess that matches more takes longer, and an attacker who measures that can work towards the secret^1. Constant-time functions are a standard defence^1.

It identifies one row and no other^1, and the database enforces it: an insert that would repeat a value is refused^1. That refusal is what lets a table remember each request key once.

blocks.text: Something is random when nothing known beforehand can predict it. One toss of a fair coin can’t be called, yet over many tosses about half come up heads. Programs use random choices so that many machines, each choosing on its own, don’t all choose the same thing.

Two hundred servers restart together after an update, and each checks for work every 60 seconds. Their timers start in the same second, so every check lands in the same second, every minute. Nothing the servers share can tell them apart. A delay each picks at random, from nothing they share, is the cheapest way to break the tie.

Randomness belongs to how a value is chosen, not to the value itself. A single random event can’t be predicted, but when the probability of each outcome is known, how often each turns up over many trials can be.^1 A uniform choice gives every outcome in a range the same chance. So many uniform choices, made apart, fill the range evenly on average, with no outcome favoured.

Computers follow their instructions exactly, so most of their random numbers are pseudorandom: a rule turns a starting value, the seed, into numbers that look random. Whoever knows the seed and the rule can work out every number.^1 Python’s generator is the Mersenne Twister, one of the most thoroughly tested there is.^2 Reuse its seed and the same sequence comes back from run to run, as long as several threads aren’t running.^2

The 200 servers each pick a start delay at random, uniformly between 0 and 60 seconds. On average 10 land in each 3-second stretch of the minute. One run might put 5 in one stretch and 16 in another, because random choices clump by chance. No stretch gets anything like all 200, and that is the point: the checks spread across the minute instead of landing in one second.

Looking random isn’t the same as being unpredictable. A pseudorandom sequence can pass every test of how random it looks, yet it comes from a rule. The Mersenne Twister, being completely deterministic, is completely unsuitable for cryptographic purposes.^2 For spreading out timers that doesn’t matter, since nobody gains by guessing the next delay. For a password-reset token, it does.

A random choice is useful because it carries no information. Two servers that each pick a delay at random land together only by chance, and nobody had to agree on anything to make that so. Any rule they all follow, such as starting on the minute, lines them all up instead.

Random isn’t even: choices made at random clump by chance, so a spread that must be exactly even needs a rule, not a draw. And a value someone gains by guessing needs a secure source. The pseudo-random generators of Python’s `random` module shouldn’t be used for security purposes.^2 Its `secrets` module is the one for passwords, account authentication and security tokens.^3

Where machines must spread out the same way every time, give each a delay from something it already has, such as a hash of its name. For scheduled work, one practice is a consistent method that gives each host the same number every time, so an overload or a race condition happens the same way, in a pattern.^4 Pick randomness when there is no such value, or when the spread should differ from run to run.

blocks.text: The thundering herd problem happens when a large number of waiting processes or threads are woken at the same moment, often by one event, but only one of them can use what they were waiting for^1. The rest fail and go back to waiting, and the needless waking burns CPU and other resources^1. The same pattern swamps services when many clients retry in step.

A service comes back after a 30-second outage. Ten thousand clients that failed during it all retry on the same fixed schedule and arrive in the same instant. The service falls over again under the spike, and the cycle repeats. Or 64 worker threads wait on one socket; a single connection arrives, all 64 wake, and one wins.

Three things combine: many waiters on one event, an event that releases them all together through synchronization, and a resource that only one or a few can use at a time, which creates contention. When the event fires, only one waiter can respond, so most fail and go back to sleep^1. The shared resource becomes the performance bottleneck at exactly that moment.

Between machines it appears as retries in lockstep. Clients that back off on the same schedule stay together: even with [[exponential backoff]], there are still clusters of calls^2. In caches it is a cache stampede: when a popular cached page expires under very heavy load, many servers may try to rebuild it at once^3, none knowing the others are doing the same^3.

The cures break the synchrony. Wake one waiter, not all: Linux added the `EPOLLEXCLUSIVE` flag to epoll in kernel version 4.5 so that only one of several waiting sets is woken^1. Or add randomness: [[jitter]] in the waits between retries breaks the synchronisation across clients^1, spreading the spikes towards a roughly constant rate^2. For caches, let one caller refresh an entry while the others use the old value or wait.

Say 10,000 clients fail together and retry after exactly 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds. Each retry wave puts all 10,000 requests into the same few milliseconds. If each client instead waits a random time between zero and its backoff, the 10,000 retries of the 8-second round spread across 8 seconds, about 1,250 a second. The server sees a steady stream instead of a wall.

It's easy to think exponential backoff alone prevents a herd. Backoff does make calls less and less frequent^2, but clients that failed together still retry together, leaving clusters of calls^2. Backoff needs jitter to scatter the clients as well as slow them down.

The cost lies in the timing, not the amount of work. A server that handles 1,000 requests a second copes with 10,000 spread over ten seconds, not 10,000 in one. Anything that makes clients act in step, such as a shared timer, a single wake-up or one expiry time, turns average load into peak load. Marc Brooker of AWS argues that jittered backoff repays its small cost so well that it should be a standard approach for remote clients^2.

Jitter spreads work but doesn't remove it: none of the jittered approaches changes the fundamental way work grows with contention, though they cut it substantially at reasonable levels^2. Waking only one waiter can leave capacity idle if that one is slow. And randomised timing makes behaviour harder to reproduce in tests.

Where the herd can't be scattered at its source, the resource can protect itself. A queue in front of it admits work at the rate it can handle; [[rate limiting]] caps how fast each client may call; and load shedding refuses excess requests quickly instead of letting them pile up.

A surge of real users, such as the opening minute of a ticket sale, also swamps a service. But those users arrive because of something outside the system, not because the system put them in step. A thundering herd is synchrony the system creates, so scattering the timing fixes it; a genuine surge needs more capacity or a queue.

claims.text: The thundering herd problem occurs when many processes or threads are woken at once, but only one can respond.

quotes.text: The thundering herd problem is a performance-degrading phenomenon in computer science and computer networking that occurs when a large number of processes or threads are simultaneously awakened, typically in response to a specific event or the availability of a resource. However, only one process is able to respond to the event or access the new resource, causing most other processes to fail and go back to sleep.

claims.words: The thundering herd problem happens when a large number of waiting processes or threads are woken at the same moment, often by one event, but only one of them can use what they were waiting for

claims.text: The unnecessary awakening consumes CPU and other system resources.

quotes.text: This unnecessary awakening consumes CPU and other system resources, potentially reducing the system's overall performance and efficiency.

claims.words: the needless waking burns CPU and other resources

claims.text: Only one process can respond, so most others fail and go back to sleep.

quotes.text: However, only one process is able to respond to the event or access the new resource, causing most other processes to fail and go back to sleep.

claims.words: only one waiter can respond, so most fail and go back to sleep

claims.text: With un-jittered exponential backoff there are still clusters of calls.

quotes.text: The problem also stands out: there are still clusters of calls.

claims.words: even with exponential backoff, there are still clusters of calls

claims.text: Under very heavy load, when a cached page expires, multiple threads may try to render it simultaneously.

quotes.text: However, under very heavy load, when the cached version of that page expires, there may be sufficient concurrency in the server farm that multiple threads of execution will all attempt to render the content of that page simultaneously.

claims.words: when a popular cached page expires under very heavy load, many servers may try to rebuild it at once

claims.text: None of the concurrent servers know the others are rendering at the same time.

quotes.text: Systematically, none of the concurrent servers know that the others are doing the same rendering at the same time.

claims.words: none knowing the others are doing the same

claims.text: Linux 4.5 added the EPOLLEXCLUSIVE flag so only one of several waiting epoll sets is woken.

quotes.text: For epoll() in version 4.5 of the Linux kernel, the EPOLLEXCLUSIVE flag was added. Thus several epoll sets (different threads or different processes) may wait on the same resource and only one set will be woken up.

claims.words: Linux added the EPOLLEXCLUSIVE flag to epoll in kernel version 4.5 so that only one of several waiting sets is woken

claims.text: Jitter can be added to backoff to break the synchronisation across clients.

quotes.text: In order to avoid the thundering herd problem, jitter can be purposefully introduced in order to break the synchronization across the clients, thereby avoiding collisions.

claims.words: jitter in the waits between retries breaks the synchronisation across clients

claims.text: Jitter aims to spread out the spikes of calls to an approximately constant rate.

quotes.text: The time series above makes a great case for jitter – we want to spread out the spikes to an approximately constant rate.

claims.words: spreading the spikes towards a roughly constant rate

claims.text: Exponential backoff makes calls less and less frequent, but clusters of calls remain.

quotes.text: It’s obvious that the exponential backoff is working, in that the calls are happening less and less frequently.
The problem also stands out: there are still clusters of calls.

claims.words: Backoff does make calls less and less frequent, but clients that failed together still retry together, leaving clusters of calls

claims.text: The return on implementation complexity of jittered backoff is huge, and it should be a standard approach for remote clients.

quotes.text: The return on implementation complexity of using jittered backoff is huge, and it should be considered a standard approach for remote clients.

claims.words: Marc Brooker of AWS argues that jittered backoff repays its small cost so well that it should be a standard approach for remote clients

claims.text: None of the jitter approaches fundamentally changes how work grows with contention, but they substantially reduce work at reasonable contention.

quotes.text: It’s worth noting that none of these approaches fundamentally change the N2 nature of the work to be done, but do substantially reduce work at reasonable levels of contention.

claims.words: none of the jittered approaches changes the fundamental way work grows with contention, though they cut it substantially at reasonable levels

blocks.text: **Something grows exponentially when it grows by the same multiple each step, so the bigger it is, the faster it grows.**
Its rate of growth is proportional to its present size^1. It can start slowly: exponential doesn’t mean fast^1.

claims.text: An exponentially growing quantity grows at a rate proportional to its size.

quotes.text: The quantity grows at a rate directly proportional to its present size.

claims.words: Its rate of growth is proportional to its present size

claims.text: Something growing exponentially can be growing slowly at first.

quotes.text: Indeed, something that grows exponentially can in fact be growing slowly at first.

claims.words: It can start slowly

blocks.text: **A circuit breaker stops calling a service that keeps failing, for a while, instead of trying it again and again.**

Like the switch in a fuse box, it opens after enough failures, and calls fail at once without being sent; after a pause it lets one through to see whether the service is back. It spots a service that has stopped answering and stops the repeated tries^1, which a fixed timeout can only do slowly^1. It is usually used together with retries and timeouts^1.

claims.text: A circuit breaker identifies unresponsive services and prevents repeated attempts.

quotes.text: the Circuit Breaker pattern can proactively identify unresponsive services and can prevent repeated attempts

claims.words: It spots a service that has stopped answering and stops the repeated tries

claims.text: Timeouts can delay error responses or fail healthy requests early.

quotes.text: Unlike timeout-based methods, which can lead to delayed error responses or the premature failure of healthy requests

claims.words: which a fixed timeout can only do slowly

claims.text: Circuit breakers are used with retry, fallback and timeout.

quotes.text: The circuit breaker pattern can be used in conjunction with other patterns, such as retry, fallback, and timeout, to enhance fault tolerance in systems.

claims.words: It is usually used together with retries and timeouts

blocks.text: **A network or a service is congested when it is given more load than it can carry, and everything through it slows.**

Requests queue, some are lost, and new connections are refused^1. Retrying aggressively to make up for what was lost can keep the congestion going even after the load that caused it has gone^1. That is why clients that retry back off.

claims.text: Congestion causes queueing delay, packet loss or blocked connections.

quotes.text: Typical effects include queueing delay, packet loss or the blocking of new connections.

claims.words: Requests queue, some are lost, and new connections are refused

claims.text: Aggressive retransmission can increase congestion even after the load falls.

quotes.text: Network protocols that use aggressive retransmissions to compensate for packet loss due to congestion can increase congestion, even after the initial load has been reduced to a level that would not normally have induced network congestion.

claims.words: Retrying aggressively to make up for what was lost can keep the congestion going

blocks.text: **Rate limiting caps how many requests a service takes in a given time, and refuses the rest.**
It controls the rate of requests sent or received^1, which protects a service from floods of traffic, whether an attack or a crowd of clients retrying at once^1.

claims.text: Rate limiting controls the rate of requests sent or received.

quotes.text: rate limiting is used to control the rate of requests sent or received by a network interface controller

claims.words: It controls the rate of requests sent or received

claims.text: Rate limiting can be used to prevent denial-of-service attacks.

quotes.text: It can be used to prevent DoS attacks and limit web scraping.

claims.words: which protects a service from floods of traffic

blocks.text: **Two-phase commit is how several parties agree to make a change together: first everyone says whether they can, then everyone does it, or no one does.**

A coordinator asks every participant whether it can commit, and then tells them all to commit or all to roll back^1. It still reaches the right outcome through many temporary failures^1, though not all of them.

claims.text: Two-phase commit coordinates all participants on whether to commit or abort.

quotes.text: It is a distributed algorithm that coordinates all the processes that participate in a distributed atomic transaction on whether to commit or abort (roll back) the transaction.

claims.words: A coordinator asks every participant whether it can commit, and then tells them all to commit or all to roll back

claims.text: Two-phase commit achieves its goal even through many temporary failures.

quotes.text: achieves its goal even in many cases of temporary system failure

claims.words: It still reaches the right outcome through many temporary failures

blocks.text: **The accounting equation says what a business owns equals what it owes plus what belongs to its owners, and every entry keeps it true.**
Like any equation, its two sides are always equal^1, and it is the foundation double-entry bookkeeping is built on^1.

claims.text: Each side of the accounting equation is always equal.

quotes.text: Like any equation, each side will always be equal.

claims.words: its two sides are always equal

claims.text: The accounting equation is the foundation of double-entry bookkeeping.

quotes.text: is the foundation for the double-entry bookkeeping system and the cornerstone of accounting science

claims.words: it is the foundation double-entry bookkeeping is built on

blocks.text: **Pseudorandom numbers come from a rule that makes them look random, though they aren’t.**
They appear statistically random while being produced by a deterministic, repeatable process^1. The rule starts from a seed, and the same seed gives the same numbers every time^1.

claims.text: Pseudorandom sequences appear random but come from a deterministic, repeatable process.

quotes.text: A pseudorandom sequence of numbers is one that appears to be statistically random, despite having been produced by a completely deterministic and repeatable process.

claims.words: They appear statistically random while being produced by a deterministic, repeatable process

claims.text: The same seed yields the same sequence every time.

quotes.text: Since the same seed will yield the same sequence every time

claims.words: the same seed gives the same numbers every time

blocks.text: **A hash function turns data of any size into a short value of fixed size.**
It maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, called hashes^1. The same input always gives the same hash, which is what lets a hash stand for the data it came from.

claims.text: A hash function maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values.

quotes.text: A hash function is any function that can be used to map data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values

claims.words: It maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, called hashes
